This screenshot shows the Blob side is configured correctly, but there’s one important issue with TiDB.

Your Blob variables are good and available to both environments:

- `BLOB_WEBHOOK_PUBLIC_KEY` → Production and Preview
- `BLOB_STORE_ID` → Production and Preview
- `BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN` → Production and Preview

That means the Blob connection is ready.

The problem is your TiDB variables are currently scoped only to:

`Production`

I can see:

- `TIDB_HOST` → Production
- `TIDB_PORT` → Production
- `TIDB_USER` → Production
- `TIDB_PASSWORD` → Production
- `TIDB_DATABASE` → Production

Since you want to test a **Preview deployment**, those variables need to be available in **Preview** too.

For each `TIDB_*` variable, click the `...` menu on the right, edit the environment scope, and change it from:

```text
Production
```

to:

```text
Production and Preview
```

Do that for all five TiDB variables.

After that, your environment list should effectively look like:

```text
BLOB_WEBHOOK_PUBLIC_KEY   Production and Preview
BLOB_STORE_ID             Production and Preview
BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN     Production and Preview

TIDB_HOST                 Production and Preview
TIDB_PORT                 Production and Preview
TIDB_USER                 Production and Preview
TIDB_PASSWORD             Production and Preview
TIDB_DATABASE             Production and Preview
```

Then redeploy the latest Preview deployment.

One caveat: because you enabled **TiDB Branching**, the integration may manage Preview credentials dynamically. If Vercel/TiDB does not let you simply enable Preview on those same five variables, don’t manually copy production DB credentials into Preview. In that case, go back to the TiDB integration and verify the branching configuration is creating Preview-specific variables automatically.

But based on this screenshot, the immediate issue is clear: **Blob is ready; TiDB is still Production-only.**

Yes — I’d make the CLI a first-class part of the plan, not just an optional afterthought. ## Updated plan ### 1. Public website Build a public website where users can enter either: ```text utkarsh-wadalkar ``` or: ```text https://whoburnedmore.com/u/utkarsh-wadalkar ``` The site should normalize the input, validate the profile, fetch the public stats, and show live previews. Supported styles: ```text Landscape Hero Report ``` ### 2. Live card API Expose dynamic endpoints such as: ```text /api/card/:handle/landscape.svg /api/card/:handle/hero.svg /api/card/:handle/report.svg ``` Example: ```text https://yourdomain.com/api/card/utkarsh-wadalkar/landscape.svg ``` The SVG should be generated dynamically from the latest profile data, so the user does not have to regenerate or edit their README when stats change. ### 3. Card generator UI After entering the handle, show: ```text Live Preview [ Landscape ] [ Hero ] [ Report ] ``` Then generate four outputs. #### Direct card URL ```text https://yourdomain.com/api/card/utkarsh-wadalkar/landscape.svg ``` #### GitHub Markdown ```md [![WhoBurnedMore](https://yourdomain.com/api/card/utkarsh-wadalkar/landscape.svg)](https://whoburnedmore.com/u/utkarsh-wadalkar) ``` #### HTML ```html ``` #### CLI ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar ``` Every output gets a **Copy** button. --- ## 4. CLI package Create a small npm CLI package: ```text whoburnedmore-card ``` Users can run: ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar ``` and receive something like: ```text WhoBurnedMore Card Handle: utkarsh-wadalkar Style: landscape Direct URL: https://yourdomain.com/api/card/utkarsh-wadalkar/landscape.svg GitHub Markdown: [![WhoBurnedMore](https://yourdomain.com/api/card/utkarsh-wadalkar/landscape.svg)](https://whoburnedmore.com/u/utkarsh-wadalkar) ``` The CLI should also support profile URLs: ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card https://whoburnedmore.com/u/utkarsh-wadalkar ``` and style selection: ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar --style hero ``` ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar --style report ``` I'd also support: ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar --format markdown ``` ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar --format html ``` ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar --format url ``` And a convenient copy option: ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar --copy ``` So the complete CLI interface can remain very small: ```text whoburnedmore-card --style landscape|hero|report --format markdown|html|url --copy ``` --- ## 5. Website should generate CLI commands too On the website, the CLI section can automatically reflect the selected style. For example, if the user selects **Hero**: ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar --style hero ``` If they select **Report**: ```bash npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar --style report ``` So website users can choose either workflow: ```text Paste into README or Run in terminal ``` --- ## 6. Recommended repository structure I would use a monorepo: ```text whoburnedmore-card/ │ ├── apps/ │ └── web/ │ ├── app/ │ │ ├── page.tsx │ │ ├── generate/ │ │ └── api/ │ │ └── card/ │ │ └── [handle]/ │ │ └── [style]/ │ │ └── route.ts │ │ │ ├── components/ │ │ ├── HandleInput.tsx │ │ ├── CardPreview.tsx │ │ ├── StyleSelector.tsx │ │ └── CopySnippet.tsx │ │ │ └── lib/ │ ├── handle.ts │ ├── stats.ts │ └── svg/ │ ├── packages/ │ ├── core/ │ │ ├── handle.ts │ │ ├── urls.ts │ │ └── types.ts │ │ │ └── cli/ │ ├── src/ │ │ └── index.ts │ └── package.json │ ├── package.json ├── tsconfig.json └── README.md ``` The important part is having: ```text packages/core ``` for shared logic. Both the website and CLI should use the same functions for: ```text handle normalization profile URL parsing style names card URL generation Markdown generation HTML generation ``` That prevents duplicated logic. --- ## 7. Keep the MVP stateless Initially, don't add: ```text Login User accounts Database Dashboard Saved cards OAuth ``` The whole system can work as: ```text WhoBurnedMore ↓ Stats fetcher ↓ Card renderer ↓ Dynamic SVG endpoint ↙ ↘ Website GitHub ↑ User input CLI ↓ Shared core package ↓ Card URL / Markdown / HTML ``` That gives you a genuinely useful product without unnecessary infrastructure. ## Final requirements section You can put this directly into your implementation plan: ```md ## Website, CLI, documentation and deployment - Scaffold the repository as a Vercel-ready TypeScript monorepo. - Build a public card-generator website where users can enter either: - a WhoBurnedMore handle; - or a full WhoBurnedMore profile URL. - Normalize and validate the provided profile input. - Show live previews for all supported card styles: - Landscape - Hero - Report - Expose dynamic SVG endpoints: /api/card/:handle/landscape.svg /api/card/:handle/hero.svg /api/card/:handle/report.svg - Cards must remain live and automatically reflect updated public profile statistics without requiring users to regenerate the card or modify their README. - For the selected card, generate copyable: - Direct SVG URL - GitHub Markdown - HTML embed - CLI command - Add one-click copy controls for every generated output. - Create an npm CLI package usable through: npx whoburnedmore-card YOUR-HANDLE - The CLI must accept either a handle or full profile URL. - Support CLI options: --style landscape|hero|report --format markdown|html|url --copy - Example: npx whoburnedmore-card utkarsh-wadalkar --style landscape --format markdown - Share handle parsing, URL generation, types, and snippet generation between the web application and CLI through a common core package. - Keep the initial product stateless: - no login; - no database; - no saved cards; - no user accounts. - Document all supported website, API, Markdown, HTML, and CLI usage in the README. - Include README snippets for every style with a replaceable handle: - Document local development, npm CLI usage, and Vercel deployment. - Deploy the web application/API to Vercel. - Publish the CLI package to npm when ready. - After production deployment, replace placeholder URLs throughout the README with the real production domain. ``` This gives the project **three ways to use the same system**: website for normal users, direct API for embedding, and CLI for developers.

Yes — TiDB can also hold website metadata, and that’s a good use of it.

But for “instant loading,” I’d still avoid making every frontend render depend directly on a fresh TiDB query. Use TiDB as the persistent source, then cache frequently read metadata at the app/CDN layer.

For example, TiDB can store things like:

```text
site_metadata
- total_cards_generated
- total_profiles
- total_requests
- featured_handles
- latest_supported_styles
- renderer_version
- maintenance_flag
- announcements
```

And maybe per-profile metadata:

```text
profile_metadata
- handle
- display_name
- avatar_url
- last_synced_at
- available_styles
- total_card_views
```

Then your website flow becomes:

```text
Browser
  ↓
Next.js page / API
  ↓
Next Data Cache
  ↓ miss
TiDB
```

So common homepage metadata gets cached and loads very quickly.

For example:

```ts
const metadata = unstable_cache(
  async () => getSiteMetadataFromTiDB(),
  ["site-metadata"],
  { revalidate: 300 }
);
```

Conceptually that gives you:

```text
TiDB = persistent truth
Next cache = fast reads
Vercel CDN = fast delivery
```

That’s better than:

```text
every page load
→ open DB connection
→ query TiDB
→ wait
```

For mostly static content like:

```text
supported card styles
docs text
CLI examples
feature descriptions
```

I would **not** store those in TiDB at all. Keep them in code, because they rarely change.

Use TiDB for metadata that actually changes, such as:

```text
card count
user/profile count
render statistics
recently generated cards
featured profiles
service status
last sync information
```

So the optimized setup is:

```text
Static website content
→ bundled with Next.js

Dynamic website metadata
→ TiDB
→ Next Data Cache

Rendered card metadata
→ TiDB

Rendered PNGs
→ Blob storage

Hot PNG responses
→ Next Data Cache / CDN
```

That gives you fast page loads without turning TiDB into a bottleneck.

One more useful thing: if you show stats like:

```text
12,481 cards generated
3,928 profiles
99.9% cache hit rate
```

don’t calculate those with expensive `COUNT(*)` queries on every page view. Maintain small aggregate rows instead, e.g.:

```text
metrics
- total_cards
- total_profiles
- total_requests
```

Then homepage loading is just a tiny single-row lookup.

So yes — **TiDB is a good fit for dynamic website metadata too**, especially since you already plan to use it for card state. I’d just put Next/Vercel caching in front of it rather than treating TiDB itself as the frontend cache.

Yes, that can work, but I would not make the database itself the primary image store.

A better pattern is:

```text
User/card key
    ↓
Database metadata
    ↓
Object/blob storage for PNG
```

For example:

```text
card_key:
utkarsh-wadalkar:landscape

database row:
handle = utkarsh-wadalkar
style = landscape
image_url = ...
stats_hash = abc123
updated_at = ...
```

The actual ~197 KB PNG should live in blob/object storage, not inside PostgreSQL unless you have a specific reason.

When the same user's stats change, your flow can be:

```text
Request card
   ↓
Fetch current WhoBurnedMore stats
   ↓
Create deterministic stats hash
   ↓
Compare with cached hash

same hash
   → return existing PNG immediately

different hash
   → render new PNG
   → upload new PNG
   → update DB pointer/hash
   → delete previous PNG
   → return new PNG
```

That is a very solid architecture.

The important part is: **do not regenerate just because a request arrives**. Regenerate only when the source stats have actually changed.

A key could be:

```text
sha256({
  handle,
  style,
  relevantStats,
  rendererVersion
})
```

I would include `rendererVersion`, because if you redesign the card but the user's stats stay the same, you still want a new render.

Something like:

```text
handle: utkarsh-wadalkar
style: landscape
stats_hash: 4c6f...
renderer_version: 3
storage_key: cards/utkarsh-wadalkar/landscape/4c6f....png
```

Then the live README URL remains stable:

```text
https://whoburnedmore-card.vercel.app/api/card/utkarsh-wadalkar/landscape.png
```

but internally it can serve:

```text
cards/utkarsh-wadalkar/landscape/4c6f....png
```

That gives you two useful layers:

```text
Stable public URL
        ↓
DB/cache lookup
        ↓
Immutable versioned PNG
```

For your specific Vercel deployment, though, I would compare this against simply using Next's Data Cache.

Your current idea:

```text
Next Data Cache
```

is simpler and probably enough for the first version.

Database + blob storage gives you more control if you later want:

```text
persistent cards across deployments
cache analytics
manual invalidation
card history
CDN-backed immutable images
storage independent of framework cache behavior
multiple render workers
```

But it adds more infrastructure.

So I would use this progression:

1. **Now:** Next Data Cache for completed rendered PNGs.
2. Add a deterministic cache key based on handle/style/stats/version.
3. Only if you start hitting cache persistence/eviction/visibility problems, move the actual PNGs to object storage.
4. Keep metadata in a DB only when you genuinely need metadata/state.

If you do add persistence, I'd choose something like:

```text
Postgres / Supabase
    → metadata only

Vercel Blob / Cloudflare R2 / S3
    → PNGs
```

rather than:

```text
Postgres BYTEA
    → 197 KB image blobs
```

because storing images directly in relational DB rows works, but becomes clumsier for CDN delivery and storage management.

One more improvement: instead of deleting the previous image before the new image is ready, do this atomically:

```text
render new
→ upload new
→ update pointer
→ then delete old
```

not:

```text
delete old
→ render new
```

Otherwise a failed render can temporarily leave the user with no card.

For GitHub README reliability, the strongest design is therefore:

```text
GitHub
  ↓
stable card endpoint
  ↓
fast metadata/cache lookup
  ↓
already-rendered PNG
```

with rendering happening only on a cache miss or stats change.

So yes: your database-backed idea is good, but I'd refine it to **DB for metadata + blob/object storage for images**, with Next Data Cache still sitting in front as the fastest layer.

thoughts.content: I’d use TiDB for metadata, hashes, refresh locks, and source statistics—not repeated PNG blobs. I’d store images in object storage, cache rendered URLs in Next.js, and regenerate only when hashes change. This minimizes reads, bandwidth, and write-units.

parts:
Do it in this order: **TiDB first, then Vercel Blob, then redeploy Preview**.

### 1. Connect TiDB to Vercel

Because you’re using TiDB Cloud Starter, the cleanest path is the official **TiDB Cloud → Vercel integration**. TiDB can automatically create the required environment variables for the linked Vercel project. citeturn821864search0

Go to your **Vercel Dashboard** → open your `whoburnedmore-card` project → **Integrations** and add **TiDB Cloud**. During setup, select your Vercel project, TiDB organization/project, choose **Cluster**, choose the correct TiDB Starter instance/database, and select the framework your app expects. If your code expects a single `DATABASE_URL`, choose the Prisma/serverless-driver style if offered, because that integration creates `DATABASE_URL` automatically. citeturn821864search0

After connecting, go back to:

```text
Vercel project
→ Settings
→ Environment Variables
```

You want to see:

```text
DATABASE_URL
```

and make sure it applies to **Preview**.

If the integration gives you separate values instead:

```text
TIDB_HOST
TIDB_PORT
TIDB_USER
TIDB_PASSWORD
TIDB_DATABASE
```

but your app specifically expects `DATABASE_URL`, you can manually add one using TiDB's connection details. TiDB documents the Vercel-compatible format as:

```text
mysql://USER:PASSWORD@ENDPOINT:PORT/DATABASE?sslaccept=strict
```

TiDB Starter requires TLS when using the public endpoint. citeturn821864search0turn821864search2

Do **not** send that value here.

---

### 2. Create the Vercel Blob store

Now in Vercel, open the same project and go to the **Storage** area.

Create a new **Blob** store and choose:

```text
Public
```

for this project, because these are public GitHub README card images.

Connect that Blob store to your `whoburnedmore-card` project.

When a Blob store is connected to a Vercel project, Vercel supplies the SDK authentication environment variable:

```text
BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN
```

Vercel documents that this token is automatically added when the Blob store is linked to the project. citeturn821864search1

Then verify under:

```text
Project
→ Settings
→ Environment Variables
```

that you now have:

```text
BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN
```

and that it is available to **Preview**.

---

### 3. Verify both variables are scoped to Preview

At this point, under **Settings → Environment Variables**, you should have:

```text
DATABASE_URL
BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN
```

Both need **Preview** enabled.

Vercel lets each environment variable be scoped separately to Production, Preview, and Development. citeturn821864search3

For now I would configure:

```text
DATABASE_URL
✓ Preview
✓ Production   ← optional now, but useful soon

BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN
✓ Preview
✓ Production   ← optional now, but useful soon
```

If you specifically want to test everything before production, Preview-only is fine initially.

---

### 4. Important: redeploy after adding the variables

Adding environment variables does **not** modify an already-running deployment.

Vercel requires a new deployment for newly added environment variables to take effect. citeturn821864search3

Go to:

```text
Project
→ Deployments
→ latest Preview deployment
→ ⋯
→ Redeploy
```

Or push another commit to the preview branch.

After redeploying, the function should see:

```ts
process.env.DATABASE_URL
process.env.BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN
```

---

### 5. Verify from the deployment logs

Open the new Preview deployment:

```text
Deployments
→ Preview deployment
→ Logs
```

You should no longer see errors like:

```text
DATABASE_URL is missing
```

or:

```text
BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN is missing
```

You should instead see database initialization/migration or Blob initialization succeeding.

Do **not** log the actual environment-variable values.

Good:

```ts
console.log("DATABASE_URL configured:", Boolean(process.env.DATABASE_URL));
console.log(
  "BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN configured:",
  Boolean(process.env.BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN)
);
```

Bad:

```ts
console.log(process.env.DATABASE_URL);
console.log(process.env.BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN);
```

---

### 6. One thing to check with TiDB migrations

If your deployment runs something like:

```bash
prisma migrate deploy
```

or your own schema setup, verify the database actually exists in TiDB first.

In TiDB Cloud:

```text
My TiDB
→ your Starter instance
→ Connect
```

The connection dialog gives you the username, password, endpoint, port and database details. citeturn821864search5

Your app should then create/use the tables we discussed for things such as:

```text
card_cache
profile_cache
service_metrics
usage_hourly
```

depending on what your current implementation has actually created.

---

### 7. Final expected setup

You should end up with:

```text
Vercel Project
│
├── Preview deployment
│
├── Environment Variables
│   ├── DATABASE_URL
│   │      ↓
│   │   TiDB Cloud Starter
│   │
│   └── BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN
│          ↓
│       Public Vercel Blob
│
├── Next.js app
│
├── TiDB
│   ├── card metadata
│   ├── hashes
│   ├── render state
│   └── status/usage metrics
│
└── Vercel Blob
    └── persistent PNG cards
```

For your architecture, **do not create a private Blob store**. The generated PNGs are intended to be fetched by GitHub READMEs, so public Blob storage is the appropriate choice. citeturn821864search1

One more useful check: after everything is connected, test the Preview URL by generating your own `utkarsh-wadalkar` Landscape card first. That should exercise **TiDB → renderer → Vercel Blob → cache → image endpoint** end-to-end before you point GitHub at it.

Done. I updated the ideation document so the **Knowledge Graph is now the core intelligence layer**, not just an extra technology.

The PDF now includes the complete KG concept we discussed: **KG node/relationship schema, graph-based skill-gap reasoning, beneficiary example, NSQF/NQR graph integration, explainable recommendation paths, Neo4j/Cypher implementation, multilingual architecture, revised novelty, MVP scope, evaluation metrics, and the complete system architecture**.

### Updated PDF
[**Download SIH26097 - Knowledge Graph Final Year Project Ideation**](sandbox:/mnt/data/SIH26097_Knowledge_Graph_Final_Year_Project_Ideation.pdf)

The central project positioning is now:

> **Voice Input → Multilingual Understanding → Beneficiary Knowledge Graph → Livelihood & NSQF Knowledge Graph → Graph-Based Skill-Gap Reasoning → Local Opportunity Ranking → Explainable Recommendation → Voice Output**

This should make the **AI & DS contribution** much clearer when you present the idea to your sir.
**Domain: Intelligent Skill Development & Livelihood Recommendation Systems**

thoughts.summary: Searched research on skill gaps, multilingual guidance, and career recommendations

parts:
Yes. I searched **IEEE Xplore specifically** for papers that map closely to your project: **Knowledge Graph + skill-gap analysis + career/skilling recommendation + multilingual/voice interaction**.

These are the strongest IEEE papers I found:

1. **AI-Powered Skill Gap Analysis and Career Path Recommendation System**  
   This is very close to your project because it focuses on **skill-gap analysis and career-path recommendation**, and the IEEE result explicitly mentions **knowledge graph visualization**.  
   urlIEEE Xplore paperhttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11634695/

2. **Skill-Based Recommender System for Internship and Industry Hiring using Knowledge Graphs**  
   Introduces a **knowledge-graph-driven recommender framework** representing skills, job roles, and opportunities as interconnected entities. This strongly supports your proposed graph schema.  
   urlIEEE Xplore paperhttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11354307/

3. **Development of a Knowledge Graph-Based Model for Recommendation**  
   Uses **heterogeneous knowledge graphs** to bridge skills/competencies and job recommendations, including suggestions for additional courses. Very relevant to your **current skill → missing skill → training → job** pipeline.  
   urlIEEE Xplore paperhttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10804810/  
   urlDirect IEEE PDFhttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/iel8/6287639/10380310/10804810.pdf

4. **Knowledge Graphs in Education and Employability**  
   This is especially useful for your literature review because it discusses how knowledge graphs can connect **education, skills and labour-market requirements** and help identify employment-market needs.  
   urlDirect IEEE PDFhttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/iel7/6287639/9668973/09840388.pdf

5. **Leveraging Knowledge Graphs for Personalized Internship Recommendations**  
   Builds personalized recommendations by integrating **course syllabi, student competencies and internship/job requirements through a knowledge graph**. Good supporting work for profile-to-opportunity matching.  
   urlIEEE Xplore paperhttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10987407/

6. **SkillBridge: A Job-Course Matching Framework Using Pre-Trained Language Models and Graph Representation**  
   Highly relevant because your architecture also needs to bridge **jobs and training courses**. This work combines pretrained language models with graph representations for job-course matching.  
   urlIEEE Xplore paperhttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11006254/

7. **Enhancing Career Matching with BERT and Graph Neural Networks**  
   Combines **BERT semantic understanding + Graph Neural Networks** to build dynamically updated career representations. Useful if later you want to make your graph-ranking layer more sophisticated than rule-based Cypher traversal.  
   urlIEEE Xplore paperhttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10985284/

8. **Sankalp: AI-Powered Career Guidance System**  
   This is one of the **closest overall matches** to your proposed application. The IEEE result specifically describes a **Voice Assistant module enabling multimodal and multilingual interaction**, and also mentions a **Knowledge Graph connecting careers, skills and subjects**.  
   urlDirect IEEE PDFhttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/iel8/6287639/10820123/11271208.pdf

9. **A Seamless ChatGPT Knowledge Plug-in for the Labour Market**  
   Focuses on improving access to labour-market information through a conversational interface. It is useful for the **LLM/conversational layer** of your system rather than the KG itself.  
   urlDirect IEEE PDFhttps://ieeexplore.ieee.org/iel8/6287639/10380310/10731911.pdf

For your **fourth-year project literature review**, I would prioritize these four:

**Sankalp** → strongest match for **voice + multilingual + career guidance + KG**.  
**AI-Powered Skill Gap Analysis and Career Path Recommendation** → strongest for **skill-gap reasoning**.  
**Knowledge Graphs in Education and Employability** → strongest academic foundation for **KG + education + labour market**.  
**Development of a Knowledge Graph-Based Model...** → strongest for **graph-based job/course recommendation**.

These give you a strong research lineage for your novelty claim:

> Existing IEEE work covers career guidance, skill-gap analysis, multilingual voice interaction, education/employability graphs and job-course matching, but your proposed system combines these around **PM-AJAY beneficiaries and NSQF/NQR-aligned livelihood pathways in Indian regional languages**.

Note that some IEEE PDFs may require institutional/IEEE access even when a direct PDF URL exists.

Yes — and I’d make the **knowledge graph a core part of the recommendation engine**, not something added just to satisfy the project requirement.

For this problem, a KG fits naturally because SIH26097 is fundamentally about connecting many related entities: a beneficiary’s education, current livelihood, skills, interests, constraints, local opportunities, job roles, NSQF levels, qualifications, NOS modules, training pathways, and self-employment/wage-employment options. The official problem explicitly asks the system to infer suitable NSQF-aligned training, skill gaps, relevant trades, and region-specific livelihood opportunities from a conversational profile. citeturn489185search1

The **National Qualification Register is especially graph-friendly** because qualifications already contain relationships such as job role, sector, NSQF level, eligibility criteria, learning modules/NOS, progression pathways, and employment opportunities. citeturn489185search4turn489185search5

A good revised architecture would be:

**User speaks → STT → profile extraction → Knowledge Graph → skill-gap reasoning → recommendation/ranking → explanation → TTS**

The KG could contain relationships like:

```text
Beneficiary
 ├── HAS_SKILL ──────────────> Welding
 ├── INTERESTED_IN ──────────> Manufacturing
 ├── HAS_EDUCATION ──────────> 10th Pass
 ├── LIVES_IN ───────────────> Pune District
 ├── PREFERS ────────────────> Wage Employment
 └── HAS_CONSTRAINT ─────────> Low Mobility


Welder Assistant
 ├── BELONGS_TO ─────────────> Manufacturing Sector
 ├── HAS_NSQF_LEVEL ─────────> Level 3
 ├── REQUIRES_SKILL ─────────> Welding Basics
 ├── REQUIRES_SKILL ─────────> Workplace Safety
 ├── ELIGIBLE_WITH ──────────> 10th Pass
 ├── PROGRESSES_TO ──────────> Welder
 └── AVAILABLE_IN ───────────> Maharashtra


Training Qualification
 ├── PREPARES_FOR ───────────> Welder Assistant
 ├── CONTAINS_NOS ───────────> NOS-001
 └── ALIGNS_WITH ────────────> NSQF Level 3
```

Then your **skill-gap analysis becomes actual graph reasoning** rather than asking an LLM to guess.

Suppose the beneficiary says:

> “I completed 10th. I help my father repair agricultural machinery. I know basic welding and want a job near my village.”

Your NLP layer extracts:

```text
Education = 10th
Skill = Basic Welding
Experience = Machinery Repair
Interest = Mechanical Work
Mobility = Local Only
EmploymentPreference = Wage Employment
```

The graph could traverse:

```text
Basic Welding
   ↓ MATCHES_SKILL

Welder Assistant
   ↓ REQUIRES

Safety Procedures
Blueprint Reading
Advanced Welding

   ↓ TRAINED_BY

NSQF Qualification X
   ↓ LEADS_TO

Welder / Fabricator
   ↓ DEMAND_IN

Local manufacturing / repair ecosystem
```

The output becomes much stronger:

> **Recommended pathway: Welder Assistant → Welder**  
> You already possess basic welding experience.  
> Missing competencies: workplace safety and blueprint interpretation.  
> You satisfy the education requirement.  
> This pathway is aligned with an NSQF-recognized qualification and matches your preference for nearby wage employment.

That is explainable because the answer is backed by explicit graph relationships.

### What I would change in your project novelty

Your current PDF describes the recommendation system mainly as:

**profile → skill gap → NSQF retrieval → local opportunity matching → ranking**

I would upgrade it to:

**Multilingual Voice AI + Livelihood Knowledge Graph + Graph-Based Skill-Gap Reasoning + Explainable Recommendation**

The strongest novelty statement would be:

> **A multilingual voice-first livelihood intelligence system that converts conversational beneficiary profiles into a structured knowledge graph and performs graph-based reasoning across skills, NSQF qualifications, occupations, progression pathways and regional livelihood opportunities to generate explainable skilling recommendations.**

That sounds substantially more like a serious **AI & Data Science final-year project** than a conventional voice chatbot.

For the KG itself, I would model roughly these core node types:

| Node | Example |
|---|---|
| `Beneficiary` | User-001 |
| `Skill` | Welding |
| `Interest` | Automotive Repair |
| `Occupation` | Welder |
| `Qualification` | NSQF Welder Qualification |
| `NSQFLevel` | Level 3 |
| `NOS` | Welding Safety NOS |
| `Sector` | Manufacturing |
| `EducationLevel` | 10th Pass |
| `Location` | Pune |
| `LivelihoodOpportunity` | Fabrication Workshop |
| `EmploymentType` | Wage Employment |
| `TrainingProvider` | Training Centre |

And relationships such as:

```text
HAS_SKILL
INTERESTED_IN
LIVES_IN
HAS_EDUCATION
PREFERS_EMPLOYMENT
REQUIRES_SKILL
HAS_QUALIFICATION
ALIGNED_WITH
BELONGS_TO_SECTOR
HAS_NOS
PROGRESSES_TO
QUALIFIES_FOR
AVAILABLE_IN
HAS_OPPORTUNITY_IN
TRAINED_BY
SIMILAR_TO
```

The NQR is useful here because its official records already expose eligibility, progression pathways, learning modules/NOS and NSQF levels, which gives you real graph edges instead of inventing a taxonomy. citeturn489185search5turn489185search7

For implementation, I would use **Neo4j** for the final-year project. It is easier to demonstrate visually to your guide because you can literally show the beneficiary node connected to skills, jobs and NSQF qualifications. You also get Cypher queries that make your recommendation logic understandable.

For example:

```cypher
MATCH (u:Beneficiary {id: $user_id})-[:HAS_SKILL]->(s:Skill)
MATCH (job:Occupation)-[:REQUIRES_SKILL]->(s)
MATCH (q:Qualification)-[:PREPARES_FOR]->(job)
MATCH (q)-[:ALIGNED_WITH]->(level:NSQFLevel)
WHERE q.minEducation <= u.educationLevel
RETURN job, q, level
```

Then calculate missing competencies:

```cypher
MATCH (u:Beneficiary {id: $user_id})
MATCH (job:Occupation {id: $job_id})-[:REQUIRES_SKILL]->(required:Skill)
WHERE NOT (u)-[:HAS_SKILL]->(required)
RETURN required
```

This gives you a clean distinction:

**LLM/AI does understanding.  
Knowledge Graph stores domain knowledge and relationships.  
Graph reasoning determines valid pathways.  
Ranking chooses the best pathway.  
LLM converts the result into natural Marathi/Hindi/English.**

That separation is also safer than letting an LLM invent NSQF recommendations.

I would therefore update your system flow in the PDF to:

**Voice Input → Language Detection/STT → Conversational Profile Extraction → Beneficiary Knowledge Graph → NSQF/NQR Knowledge Graph → Graph-Based Skill Gap & Path Reasoning → Local Opportunity Ranking → Explainable Recommendation → TTS**

And I’d rename the central component from **“NSQF/NQR Retrieval”** to **“Livelihood & NSQF Knowledge Graph”**.

This addition actually strengthens your original project substantially rather than changing its direction. Your uploaded ideation PDF currently positions the system around voice profiling, skill-gap analysis and NSQF-aligned recommendations; a KG becomes the structured intelligence layer connecting those pieces. fileciteturn0file0L35-L63

If this is what your sir specifically expects, the next PDF version should make **Knowledge Graph Architecture, KG Schema, Graph-Based Recommendation, and KG Novelty** visibly central instead of mentioning KG only as part of the tech stack.

thoughts.summary: Searched research on multilingual knowledge graph career guidance systems

parts:
I used Firecrawl’s research-paper index and searched the topic from three angles: **knowledge-graph skill matching**, **career/education recommendation**, and **multilingual voice access for low-digital-literacy users**. The best papers for your SIH26097 + Knowledge Graph project are below.

- **KG-First, LLM-Fallback: A Hybrid Microservice for Grounded Skill Search and Explanation** — arXiv:2605.01582. This is probably the **closest paper to your proposed architecture** because it explicitly combines authoritative competency frameworks with a **knowledge graph first, LLM fallback** approach for grounded skill search and explanations. Very useful for justifying why your system should keep NSQF/NQR facts in the graph and use an LLM only for understanding/explanation.  
  Download/search: urlarXiv paperhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01582  
  PDF: urlDownload PDFhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.01582

- **Job Posting-Enriched Knowledge Graph for Skills-based Matching** — arXiv:2109.02554. This paper directly addresses the idea that job seekers possess some skills while occupations require others, and that reducing the **skill gap** improves job fit. It is highly relevant to your graph relation design: `HAS_SKILL`, `REQUIRES_SKILL`, occupation matching, and gap computation.  
  Download/search: urlarXiv paperhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2109.02554  
  PDF: urlDownload PDFhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.02554

- **Community-Based Data Integration of Course and Job Data in Support of Personalized Career-Education Recommendations** — arXiv:2006.13864. This one is especially useful for your **training → skills → job/livelihood** pathway because it integrates course descriptions and job data while explicitly discussing skill mismatch between what courses teach and what jobs require.  
  Download/search: urlarXiv paperhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2006.13864  
  PDF: urlDownload PDFhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.13864

- **HRGraph: Leveraging LLMs for HR Data Knowledge Graphs with Information Propagation-based Job Recommendation** — arXiv:2408.13521. This is strong support for using a KG for job matching, skill relationships, learning-gap identification, and recommendation. It also helps justify combining **LLMs + graph reasoning** rather than choosing only one.  
  Download/search: urlarXiv paperhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2408.13521  
  PDF: urlDownload PDFhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.13521

- **Explicit Knowledge Graph Reasoning for Conversational Recommendation** — arXiv:2305.00783. This is valuable for the **voice conversation → clarification → recommendation** part of your project. The paper studies conversational recommendation where the system asks questions to understand current user preferences and explicitly reasons over a knowledge graph.  
  Download/search: urlarXiv paperhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00783  
  PDF: urlDownload PDFhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.00783

- **JobSphere: An AI-Powered Multilingual Career Copilot for Government Employment Platforms** — arXiv:2511.08343. This is one of the most relevant papers for your **Indian multilingual government-employment use case**. It addresses navigation complexity, limited language options, personalized support, government employment systems, and supports **English, Hindi and Punjabi**. This is strong literature support for your Marathi + Hindi + English MVP.  
  Download/search: urlarXiv paperhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08343  
  PDF: urlDownload PDFhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.08343

- **Labour Market Information Driven, Personalized, OER Recommendation System for Lifelong Learners** — arXiv:2005.07465. This one supports your idea of combining **labour-market demand + skill decomposition + learning recommendations**. It extracts skills demanded by jobs and recommends learning content to help users progress toward those skills.  
  Download/search: urlarXiv paperhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2005.07465  
  PDF: urlDownload PDFhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.07465

- **LLM-Assisted Knowledge Graph Completion for Curriculum and Domain Modelling in Personalized Higher Education Recommendations** — arXiv:2501.12300. This is useful if you want to explain how an LLM could help **populate or complete your KG**, while the graph remains the structured source for recommendation.  
  Download/search: urlarXiv paperhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12300  
  PDF: urlDownload PDFhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.12300

- **Towards Explainable Job Title Matching: Leveraging Semantic Textual Relatedness and Knowledge Graphs** — arXiv:2509.09522. Useful for the **explainability** argument: dense semantic matching alone may miss domain relationships, while a KG can improve both alignment and interpretability.  
  Download/search: urlarXiv paperhttps://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09522  
  PDF: urlDownload PDFhttps://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.09522

- **C3-IoC: A Career Guidance System for Assessing Student Skills using Machine Learning and Network Visualisation** — PMC9715283. This paper is useful for the broader career-guidance angle because it maps education, skills and experience to career possibilities using a knowledge base and network visualization.  
  Full text: urlPMC articlehttps://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9715283/

For your **literature review**, I would make these your core three:

1. **KG-First, LLM-Fallback** — architecture closest to your system.  
2. **Job Posting-Enriched Knowledge Graph for Skills-based Matching** — strongest for skill-gap reasoning.  
3. **JobSphere** — strongest for multilingual career guidance in an Indian/government context.

Then use **Community-Based Data Integration...** and **HRGraph** as secondary support.

Your research-gap argument can then become very clear: existing work separately covers **knowledge-graph skill matching**, **course/job recommendation**, **multilingual career assistants**, and **conversational recommendation**, but your proposed system combines these into one India-focused pipeline:

**regional-language voice interaction → beneficiary profile → livelihood/NSQF knowledge graph → skill-gap reasoning → local opportunity-aware recommendation → explainable voice output.**

One limitation: Firecrawl’s paper index is strongest for arXiv/PubMed-style sources; it does **not guarantee complete IEEE/Scopus coverage**. So I can also run a second pass specifically against **IEEE Xplore, Springer, ScienceDirect, ACM, Semantic Scholar and Scopus-indexed publisher pages** and give you a cleaner shortlist of **peer-reviewed journal/conference papers only**, excluding preprints.

- **Knowledge Graphs & Intelligent Recommendation Systems**
- **Natural Language Processing & Conversational AI**
- **Multilingual Voice-Based Intelligent Systems**
- **AI for Skill Development & Career Guidance**
- **Knowledge-Based Systems & Semantic AI**
- **Intelligent Decision Support Systems**
- **AI for Social Impact & Digital Inclusion**
- **Semantic Web & Knowledge Engineering**
- **Graph-Based AI & Recommendation Systems**
- **Conversational AI for Livelihood & Skilling**
- **AI-Driven Education & Employability Systems**
- **Human-Centered AI & Assistive Technologies**

parts:
Yes. Since your project is more specifically about **voice-based livelihood guidance + knowledge graphs + skill recommendations**, you don't have to use the generic AI/ML domain.

Good alternatives are:

- **Knowledge Engineering & Semantic Web** — ⭐ strongest if your sir wants the **Knowledge Graph** to be the project's main technical contribution.
- **Natural Language Processing (NLP)** — suitable if multilingual voice interaction is the primary focus.
- **Intelligent Recommendation Systems** — suitable if skill-gap → NSQF course → livelihood recommendation is central.
- **Speech & Language Technology** — suitable for Marathi/Hindi/English voice-first interaction.
- **Data Science & Knowledge Engineering** — broader, but still highlights the KG.
- **AI for Social Good / Social Computing** — describes the application impact rather than the core technology.
- **Educational Technology / Skill Development Technology** — describes the skilling application domain.

### For your project, I'd use

**Domain:** **Knowledge Engineering & Semantic Web**  
**Sub-domain:** Knowledge Graphs, NLP & Recommendation Systems  
**Application Area:** Skill Development & Livelihood Guidance

This differentiates the project from the many final-year projects simply labelled **"AI/ML"**, while accurately reflecting your proposed **NSQF/Livelihood Knowledge Graph**.

parts: Give me official website of SIH for problem statement 26097. I want to write down the problem statement for my project. So give me the website of SIH so that I can verify it. You don't send me the problem statement, send me the website where that 26097 problem statement is.

Modify this above PDF according to this SIH problem statement. Search about this problem statement, about its novelty, and all the topics present in that PDF. Make give me output as a PDF. I want to present this PDF for my fourth-year project, and this PDF will act as an ideation idea presentation to my teacher.
SIH26097 solution
The problem isn't merely:
"AI recommends courses."
It's:
"A person with limited digital literacy can simply speak in their own language, and the system guides them from their current skills → skill gap → NSQF-aligned training → livelihood opportunity."
That is a much stronger product story.
And for the hackathon, I'd make Marathi + Hindi + English the MVP languages, then architect the system so additional Indian languages can be plugged in without changing the core recommendation engine. This keeps the implementation realistic while demonstrating the multilingual requirement properly.

Any other than  Domain: Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning (AI/ML)  
Suggest oneline multiple answer
What is project domain
Give all this PDF
Any other than Domain: Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning (AI/ML)

Any other than  Domain: Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning (AI/ML)
Suggest one line answer
Implementing knowledge graph in this Idea, is what sir wants

Done. I rebuilt the original two-page ideation PDF around **SIH26097**, while retaining its presentation structure: Abstract → Research Gap → Novelty → Keywords → References → Proposed System Flow. fileciteturn0file0L9-L31 fileciteturn0file0L35-L90

One important correction from the initial framing: **SIH26097 is officially about SC communities under the PM-AJAY Grant-in-Aid component, not specifically persons with visual impairment.** The problem asks for a multilingual, voice-based livelihood assistant that profiles beneficiaries, identifies skill gaps, recommends NSQF-aligned pathways, considers local opportunities, and can work through low-tech channels such as IVR, WhatsApp voice notes, mobile, or kiosks. citeturn644637search5turn784546search8

I also strengthened the final-year-project novelty around the product story you described:

**spoken aspirations → structured livelihood profile → skill-gap analysis → NSQF/NQR training → local livelihood opportunity**

The PDF includes **Marathi + Hindi + English as the realistic MVP**, a language-independent recommendation architecture, local opportunity-aware ranking, explainable recommendations, low-connectivity design, NSQF/NQR retrieval, and a bounded technical architecture suitable for a fourth-year AI & DS project. This aligns well with PM-AJAY's actual requirement that skilling reflect beneficiary interest, local skill-gap/job-market relevance, NSQF compliance, certification, and wage/self-employment outcomes. citeturn784546search0turn644637search0

### PDF
[**Download SIH26097 Final Year Project Ideation PDF**](sandbox:/mnt/data/SIH26097_Final_Year_Project_Ideation.pdf)

I named the concept **KaushalVaani — AI-Driven Voice Livelihood & NSQF Skilling Assistant** in the PDF; the name can easily be changed later if your team already has one.

parts:
For your **SIH26097 + Knowledge Graph project**, I recommend writing the project domain as:

**Domain: Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning (AI/ML)**

If your college form allows a more specific domain, use:

**Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning — Knowledge Graphs, Multilingual Voice AI & Recommendation Systems**

And if it asks for an **application area** separately:

### Users & problem  
The **24/7 Intelligent Code Reviewer** is designed for students, individual developers, engineering teams, and organizations that need fast, consistent code reviews without depending on reviewer availability. It removes the delay and inconsistency of manual reviews by automatically identifying **bugs, security issues, performance bottlenecks, readability problems, architectural violations, and optimization opportunities** across multiple programming languages. Each submission also receives a standardized **code-quality score from 1–10**, while historical reviews help developers understand how their code quality improves over time.

### Approach  
An authenticated user submits source code through the platform. The backend first detects the programming language, validates and securely prepares the submission, then retrieves relevant review patterns from previously supplied historical review data. **Gemini** analyzes the code using the submitted source, review criteria, and relevant historical examples as context. It produces a structured review containing detected issues, severity, explanation, suggested fixes, architectural recommendations, optimization opportunities, and an overall **1–10 quality rating**. The review is stored in the user's history so future submissions can be compared against earlier ones and recurring development patterns can be identified.

Historical CSV data containing fields such as `<id>`, `<type>`, and `<description>` is ingested, normalized, and stored so rules such as *avoid single-character variable names*, *cache repeated database lookups*, or *never interpolate raw user input into SQL queries* can ground and enrich future reviews.

### GCP stack  
**Gemini on Vertex AI** for multi-language code understanding, bug detection, security and architecture analysis, optimization suggestions, structured review generation, and quality scoring.  

**BigQuery** for ingesting and processing historical review datasets, storing normalized review patterns, analyzing recurring issues, and generating developer-level quality trends over time.  

**Cloud Storage** for temporary/private handling of uploaded CSV files or larger source-code submissions.  

**Firebase Authentication / Identity Platform** for secure user authentication and isolation of review histories.  

**Cloud Run** hosts the API and review-processing service, providing a serverless deployment that automatically scales with hackathon and production workloads.

### Why this data product  
**BigQuery** fits the historical-learning requirement because the system can accumulate large amounts of structured review data across users, languages, issue categories, quality scores, and timestamps. Historical CSV datasets can be loaded directly, queried efficiently, and transformed into useful patterns without maintaining a dedicated analytics infrastructure.

It also enables features beyond simple storage: identifying a developer's most common mistakes, tracking quality-score improvement, finding frequently occurring security or performance problems, and selecting relevant historical review patterns to provide Gemini with better context. This makes the reviewer **history-aware rather than a stateless LLM wrapper**.

### Edge cases  
**Authentication:** every review, source-code submission, and history record is associated with an authenticated user; users cannot access another user's submissions or review history.

**Privacy:** source code is treated as private data. Access is restricted using IAM and per-user authorization, uploads are encrypted, temporary artifacts can be automatically deleted after processing, and raw source code does not need to be exposed publicly.

**Scale:** Cloud Run automatically scales review workers based on demand, while large uploads can be processed asynchronously instead of blocking requests. Limits can be applied to file size, repository size, request frequency, and LLM usage.

**Unsupported or malformed code:** the system detects unsupported languages, binary files, empty submissions, excessively large files, generated/minified code, and incomplete snippets and returns an appropriate response instead of producing misleading reviews.

**Prompt injection inside code/comments:** source code is treated as untrusted data rather than instructions, preventing comments such as `"ignore previous instructions"` from influencing the review workflow.

**Historical-data quality:** malformed CSV rows, duplicate rules, contradictory recommendations, and irrelevant historical examples are validated and normalized before being used to ground Gemini's review.

At this prompt:

```text
Do you want to do any manual network configuration? (y/n) [n]
```

just press **Enter**.

`n` is already the default, and that’s what you want because DHCP is handling the Wi-Fi automatically.

One thing I noticed: for IPv6, Alpine seems to have picked up an address automatically. That’s fine; you do not need to change it now.

After pressing Enter, it should continue to the next setup section, likely DNS, timezone, repositories, users, SSH, and eventually disk setup.

Send me the next screen when it asks about the **disk**, because that is the point where we need to be careful and choose:

```text
/dev/sda = 59 GB SanDisk target
```

and not the HP installer USB.

Yes — exactly on that prompt.

You are currently at:

```text
localhost:/#
```

Type this exactly:

```sh
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,TRAN
```

then press **Enter**.

It should print both USB drives and their sizes/models.

We are looking for something like:

```text
NAME   SIZE  MODEL      TRAN
sda   57.8G  SanDisk    usb
sdb    7.5G  hp v236w   usb
```

The actual `sda`/`sdb` order may be different.

Send me a photo of the output after you run it. Then I’ll tell you exactly which disk name is the **SanDisk 58 GB target** before we start `setup-alpine`.

That photo is very useful. The boot entry itself is valid, and it is trying to load:

```text
/arch/boot/x86_64/vmlinuz-linux-t2
/arch/boot/x86_64/initramfs-linux-t2.img
```

Current Omarchy ISO builds are indeed using the **linux-t2 kernel for the live ISO**, even on non-Apple hardware. Omarchy’s own installer later detects whether the machine is actually T2 hardware and would use the normal `linux` kernel for a non-Apple installation. citeturn528443search1turn528443search2

There is also a current open Omarchy ISO issue saying that the live ISO’s hardcoded `linux-t2` kernel can fail on some non-Apple hardware, particularly around graphics initialization. citeturn528443search2

So the next thing I want you to try is a **one-time boot with the splash disabled and `nomodeset` added**.

On the screen you are at now, edit the command so the end changes from approximately:

```text
quiet splash xe.enable_panel_replay=0 initramfs_async=0 initrd=/arch/boot/x86_64/initramfs-linux-t2.img
```

to:

```text
nomodeset xe.enable_panel_replay=0 initramfs_async=0 initrd=/arch/boot/x86_64/initramfs-linux-t2.img
```

In other words:

```text
REMOVE:
quiet splash

ADD:
nomodeset
```

Do not change anything else.

Then press:

```text
Enter
```

This time you should see actual Linux boot messages instead of the Arch splash.

If it succeeds, great — we’ll proceed to the installer.

If it fails, the important part is that we should now get a **real error message** instead of silently returning to the menu. Take a clear photo of the last 15–20 lines.

One more thing: I do **not** recommend trying `acpi=off` yet. That can break USB, power management and other hardware on an old PC. `nomodeset` is the much safer diagnostic step first.

Good — Wi-Fi is working. You got a DHCP lease:

```text
10.191.50.93
```

Now Alpine is asking you to set the **root password**:

```text
Changing password for root
New password:
```

Type a strong password and press Enter.

Nothing will appear while you type — no stars or dots. That is normal.

Then it will ask:

```text
Retype password:
```

Type the same password again and press Enter.

After that, just continue through the next prompts. For the likely upcoming choices, use:

```text
Timezone: Asia/Kolkata
Proxy: none
SSH server: openssh
```

If it asks for a user account, create:

```text
utkarsh
```

Then when it reaches disk selection, stop and send me a photo before confirming anything. We already know the correct target is:

```text
/dev/sda = 59 GB SanDisk Cruzer Blade
```

and the installer USB is:

```text
/dev/sdb = 14 GB hp v236w
```

Yes. Based on what we’ve actually detected, your machine is from the **Intel 845G/845GL generation**, currently has about **512 MB RAM**, and the chipset itself supports **up to 2 GB of DDR200/DDR266 memory**. Intel specifies unbuffered DDR200/266 and up to 2 GB total for this chipset family. citeturn886223search21

For the graphical Xfce + XRDP setup you want, **2 GB is the target**. That would be a massive improvement over 512 MB.

Tell the shopkeeper something like:

> “I need old **DDR1 RAM**, not DDR2/DDR3. My system has an Intel 845G chipset. I need **DDR-266 / PC2100, 2.5V, non-ECC, unbuffered RAM**. Maximum system RAM is 2 GB. Prefer **1 GB low-density modules**, and please test them in the machine.”

There is one thing I **do not want you to guess**: whether your particular machine uses a full-size **184-pin desktop DIMM** or **200-pin laptop SO-DIMM**. The chipset generation supports DDR1, but the physical RAM socket depends on the actual motherboard/device. So before buying tomorrow, let's identify that exactly tonight.

From your SSH window run:

```sh
su -
```

Then:

```sh
apk add dmidecode
```

Then run:

```sh
dmidecode -t 17
```

Send me the output/photo. It should tell us things such as:

```text
Size: 512 MB
Form Factor: DIMM / SODIMM
Type: DDR
Speed: 266 MT/s
Locator: DIMM0
```

Also run:

```sh
dmidecode -t 2
```

That may reveal the exact motherboard manufacturer/model.

### If it confirms normal desktop DIMMs

Then ask for:

```text
DDR1 SDRAM
1 GB per stick
184-pin DIMM
DDR-266 / PC2100
2.5 V
Non-ECC
Unbuffered
Low-density
Prefer double-sided 16-chip module
```

The **low-density / 16-chip** detail is important for very old chipsets. A typical compatible 1 GB module uses older-density chips that the 845 memory controller understands. Intel's supported configurations include 1 GB DIMMs built from the supported 512-Mbit memory technology. citeturn886223search21

If the motherboard has **two RAM slots**, ideally get:

```text
1 GB + 1 GB = 2 GB total
```

That's the maximum I'd buy for this system. Don't buy 4 GB.

### If it says SODIMM

Then you need the laptop-sized equivalent:

```text
DDR1
1 GB
200-pin SO-DIMM
DDR-266 / PC2100
2.5 V
Non-ECC
```

So **don't purchase based only on “DDR1”**—desktop DDR1 and laptop DDR1 physically won't interchange.

Also, if the shop only has **PC2700 DDR-333 or PC3200 DDR-400**, they *may* downclock and work, but for a motherboard this old I would prefer genuine **PC2100/DDR-266** if available. Compatibility matters more than speed here.

And because DDR1 is roughly two decades old, most stock will be used/refurbished. Ask the shopkeeper to **test both sticks in your machine**, boot Alpine, and verify the full amount before you leave. If possible, take the old 512 MB stick with you.

Once we know the form factor from `dmidecode -t 17`, I can give you a **single exact one-line specification to show the shopkeeper**, with no ambiguity.

This screen confirms your motherboard is **Legacy BIOS**, and I need to correct one important thing from the earlier guide: current Omarchy 4 does **not appear to officially support Legacy BIOS installs cleanly**. There are recent Omarchy reports where the installer runs, but the installed system then fails to boot because the installer expects UEFI/Limine. citeturn654318search1turn654318search2

So before we continue, do this first:

1. Open **Hard Disk Boot Priority**.
2. Send me a photo of that screen.
3. Also try changing **First Boot Device** from `Removable` and see whether `USB-HDD` is available as an option.

Your current values are:

```text
First Boot Device   = Removable
Second Boot Device  = Hard Disk
Third Boot Device   = CDROM
Boot Other Device   = Enabled
```

For booting the installer, the likely correct Legacy BIOS setup will be:

```text
First Boot Device   = USB-HDD    ← if available
Second Boot Device  = Hard Disk
Third Boot Device   = CDROM
Boot Other Device   = Enabled
```

Then inside **Hard Disk Boot Priority**, the Omarchy installer USB should be moved above other disks.

But there is a bigger compatibility issue: Omarchy’s current official installer documentation only describes its standard ISO installation and does not document a supported Legacy-BIOS path. citeturn654318search0 A very recent user with a Legacy-BIOS PC reported installation completing but the machine failing on first boot; another user successfully worked around this by installing **GRUB in BIOS/MBR mode** after the Omarchy installation. citeturn654318search1turn654318search2

So we have two realistic paths:

- **Path A — Try Omarchy anyway:** boot the installer in Legacy mode, install to the 58 GB USB, then if it does not boot, install GRUB/i386-pc manually to that USB. This is doable, but it is an unsupported workaround.
- **Path B — Safer for this very old PC:** install plain Arch/Debian first with proper Legacy-BIOS support and build the NAS/server setup there. This is substantially less fragile.

Since your goal specifically is Omarchy, I’d still try **Path A**, but we should do it carefully.

Send me the **Hard Disk Boot Priority** screen next. I’ll tell you exactly which entry to move to the top and then we’ll test whether the Omarchy installer itself boots on this machine before touching the 58 GB target USB.

parts:
What happened is **not a normal successful boot**. The installer starts, briefly drops to a `boot:` prompt, then returns to the Syslinux menu. That usually means the BIOS-mode boot entry is failing before the Linux kernel/initramfs really starts. Arch’s Syslinux docs note that when a menu entry just refreshes/returns, it commonly indicates a boot-entry/config problem; pressing `Tab` lets you inspect/edit the selected entry’s boot parameters. citeturn238333search0

Do this next:

1. On the Omarchy menu, highlight:
   ```text
   Omarchy install medium (x86_64, BIOS)
   ```
2. Press **Tab**.
3. A long boot command should appear at the bottom.
4. **Take a clear photo of that entire line and send it to me before changing anything.**

I want to see exactly what kernel/initramfs paths Omarchy is trying to load on this old BIOS.

Also, before retrying, make sure **Caps Lock and Scroll Lock are OFF**. Syslinux can intentionally show a `boot:` prompt when certain keys such as Shift/Alt are held or lock states are set. citeturn238333search2

One other thing we can try after I see the `Tab` line is booting with older-hardware-friendly kernel parameters such as:

```text
nomodeset
```

or, depending on where it is hanging,

```text
acpi=off
```

but **don’t add those yet**. `nomodeset` is relatively safe for testing graphics initialization; `acpi=off` is much more invasive, so we should only use it if the symptoms point there.

The fact that you got the Arch/Omarchy splash means the USB itself and BIOS boot selection are basically working. The failure is happening **after Syslinux hands off to the selected Omarchy boot entry**, which is much narrower and easier to debug.

Send me the screen after pressing **Tab** on the first Omarchy option.

thoughts.content: I’m checking Omarchy’s current installation and boot expectations, then matching them to a persistent 64-GB USB root drive with optional external HDD storage. I’m also identifying reliability and flash-wear concerns that could affect this setup.

I’m distinguishing current Omarchy guidance from older tutorials. A dedicated installer medium is safest; Omarchy’s Btrfs design should be preserved, while flash wear favors an external SSD over an inexpensive thumb drive.

I’m using the current Omarchy manual rather than legacy tutorials. The ISO can target a selected drive, wipe it for full-disk installation, encrypt by default, and requires disabling Secure Boot or TPM. For unattended NAS reboots, encryption needs special planning.

I’m treating the 64-GB device as Linux’s `/` root disk, not a Windows-style C: drive. It should suit a lean system, while the external HDD should hold NAS data. A separate installer USB is the safest installation path.

thoughts.summary: Verified and sized the installation setup using current guidance

parts:
At this prompt:

```text
HTTP/FTP proxy URL? (e.g. 'http://proxy:8080', or 'none') [none]
```

just press **Enter**.

You do not need a proxy.

After that Alpine should move on to mirror/repository selection. If it asks something like:

```text
Enter mirror number (1-...)
```

choose the option for automatic/fastest mirror if offered, usually:

```text
f
```

or simply accept the default if it says it will detect the fastest mirror.

You are doing fine so far. The important disk step has not happened yet, so nothing destructive has been done.

Then you need to **swap the boot priority**.

Right now your BIOS has:

```text
1. USB-HDD0 : SanDisk     ← TARGET drive
2. USB-HDD1 : hp v236w    ← OMARCHY INSTALLER
```

Change it to:

```text
1. USB-HDD1 : hp v236w    ← FIRST
2. USB-HDD0 : SanDisk     ← SECOND
```

Use the `+` key or `Page Up` as shown on the BIOS help panel to move **hp v236w** to the top.

Then go back one screen and keep:

```text
First Boot Device  = Hard Disk
Second Boot Device = CDROM
Boot Other Device  = Enabled
```

Then press:

```text
F10
```

Choose **Yes** to save and reboot.

After reboot, the PC should boot from the **HP v236w Omarchy installer**.

Important: do **not** install or format anything until you confirm the installer actually starts. Once you see the Omarchy boot/install screen, send me a photo and I’ll guide you through selecting the **SanDisk target safely**.

Yes. For your exact hardware, I’d now switch to **Alpine Linux 3.24.1 x86 (32-bit)** and use the SanDisk as the permanent OS drive.

Your machine has only about **504 MiB RAM**, but Alpine’s documented x86 requirements are low enough for this: roughly **128 MiB for installation** and around **320 MiB for a normal system**. USB storage is supported. citeturn626679search3

## 1. Download the correct Alpine ISO

Use the **x86**, not x86_64, build.

Current stable ISO:

urlDownload Alpine Linux 3.24.1 Standard x86 ISOhttps://dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org/alpine/v3.24/releases/x86/alpine-standard-3.24.1-x86.iso

The official x86 release directory confirms `alpine-standard-3.24.1-x86.iso` is available and is about 276 MB. citeturn626679search2

Do **not** download:

```text
x86_64
aarch64
armv7
```

You need:

```text
x86
```

## 2. Re-flash your HP installer USB

On your Windows laptop, overwrite the existing Omarchy installer on the **HP v236w**.

Use balenaEtcher or Rufus.

Your drives remain:

```text
HP v236w    = temporary Alpine installer
SanDisk 58GB = permanent Alpine system disk
```

Flash:

```text
alpine-standard-3.24.1-x86.iso
```

to the HP drive.

Do not touch the SanDisk yet.

## 3. Boot using the same BIOS setup

Your BIOS configuration already works.

Keep:

```text
First Boot Device = Hard Disk
Boot Other Device = Enabled
```

Under:

```text
Hard Disk Boot Priority
```

make sure:

```text
1. HP v236w
2. SanDisk
```

Then `F10` → save and reboot.

You should get an Alpine boot screen.

Choose the normal/default Alpine boot option.

## 4. Login to the Alpine live environment

Eventually you should reach:

```text
localhost login:
```

Type:

```text
root
```

There is normally no root password in the installer environment.

You should get:

```text
localhost:~#
```

## 5. Confirm both USB drives before doing anything destructive

Run:

```sh
lsblk
```

If `lsblk` is unavailable for any reason:

```sh
fdisk -l
```

You should see two drives.

Something approximately like:

```text
/dev/sda   57.8G   SanDisk
/dev/sdb   7.5G    hp v236w
```

The names might be reversed.

Do **not** assume `/dev/sda` is SanDisk.

Identify them using size and model:

```sh
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,TRAN
```

Your target is:

```text
SanDisk ≈ 58 GB
```

## 6. Connect Ethernet

For this machine, Ethernet is strongly preferable.

Run:

```sh
ip link
```

You'll probably see something like:

```text
lo
eth0
```

or:

```text
enp2s0
```

Then:

```sh
ip addr
```

If Ethernet is connected to your router, DHCP may already work.

Test:

```sh
ping -c 3 alpine.org
```

## 7. Start Alpine setup

Run:

```sh
setup-alpine
```

It will walk you through configuration.

Use sensible values like:

```text
Keyboard layout: us
Keyboard variant: us
Hostname: home-server
```

If you prefer:

```text
Hostname: alpine-nas
```

Either is fine.

## 8. Network configuration

When asked which interface to initialize, choose your Ethernet interface, for example:

```text
eth0
```

When asked:

```text
Ip address for eth0?
```

use:

```text
dhcp
```

Do not manually assign a static IP yet.

We'll reserve one later in your router.

## 9. Root password

Set a strong root password.

You’ll need this during initial setup.

Later we’ll create a normal user.

## 10. Timezone

For India:

```text
Asia/Kolkata
```

## 11. Proxy

If it asks:

```text
HTTP/FTP proxy URL?
```

enter:

```text
none
```

or just press Enter if that is the default.

## 12. APK mirror

When Alpine asks for a package mirror, choose:

```text
f
```

if it offers automatic fastest mirror selection.

Otherwise choose a nearby mirror from the list.

## 13. Create a normal user

If it asks:

```text
Setup a user?
```

create something like:

```text
utkarsh
```

Set its password.

If asked for full name, you can leave it blank.

## 14. SSH server

When asked:

```text
Which ssh server?
```

choose:

```text
openssh
```

This is important because SSH will become your main remote-control method.

## 15. THE IMPORTANT PART — disk selection

Eventually setup asks which disk to use.

You may see something like:

```text
Available disks are:
sda
sdb
```

You want the **58 GB SanDisk**.

If you are uncertain, stop and run:

```sh
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL
```

again.

Then enter the correct target, for example:

```text
sda
```

only if `sda` is confirmed as the SanDisk.

## 16. Choose `sys` mode

Alpine supports several disk modes.

When asked:

```text
How would you like to use it?
```

choose:

```text
sys
```

For your setup, `sys` mode is simplest.

That means Alpine is fully installed onto the SanDisk like a normal OS.

You may have read about Alpine's `diskless` mode; that can reduce USB writes, and Alpine officially supports persistent diskless USB installations. citeturn626679search5

But for your first NAS build, I recommend:

```text
sys
```

because it's easier to understand and administer.

Later, if USB endurance becomes a concern, we can reconsider diskless mode.

## 17. Confirm erase

Alpine will warn you that the disk will be erased.

Triple-check:

```text
Target = SanDisk 58 GB
NOT HP v236w
```

Then confirm.

The installer will partition and install Alpine.

## 18. Reboot

When installation finishes:

```sh
reboot
```

As it restarts, remove:

```text
HP v236w installer USB
```

Leave connected:

```text
SanDisk 58 GB
```

If needed, enter BIOS and change:

```text
Hard Disk Boot Priority
```

to:

```text
1. SanDisk
```

The machine should now boot Alpine from the SanDisk.

---

## 19. Log into the installed system

You'll see something like:

```text
home-server login:
```

Login using the normal user you created or root.

Check:

```sh
df -h
```

and:

```sh
lsblk
```

You should see `/` mounted from the SanDisk.

## 20. Update Alpine

Run as root:

```sh
apk update
apk upgrade
```

Alpine uses `apk` rather than `apt` or `pacman`.

## 21. Enable SSH permanently

If you selected OpenSSH during setup, verify:

```sh
rc-service sshd status
```

Enable at boot:

```sh
rc-update add sshd
```

Start it:

```sh
rc-service sshd start
```

Get the PC's address:

```sh
ip addr
```

or:

```sh
hostname -i
```

You might see:

```text
192.168.1.105
```

## 22. Test SSH from your Windows laptop

From PowerShell:

```powershell
ssh utkarsh@192.168.1.105
```

Replace the IP with the actual one.

If that works, you've reached the most important milestone:

```text
Old PC
↓
Alpine boots
↓
SSH available
↓
you can unplug monitor/keyboard later
```

## 23. Add swap — important with only 504 MiB RAM

Your machine has very little RAM, so I strongly recommend around **1 GB swap**.

Check:

```sh
free -h
```

If no swap exists, create one:

```sh
dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=1024
chmod 600 /swapfile
mkswap /swapfile
swapon /swapfile
```

Verify:

```sh
free -h
```

Then add to `/etc/fstab`:

```text
/swapfile none swap sw 0 0
```

This won't make the machine fast, but it will reduce out-of-memory crashes.

## 24. Shut down and connect your external HDD

Run:

```sh
poweroff
```

Connect the external HDD.

Then boot again.

Run:

```sh
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,LABEL,MODEL,MOUNTPOINTS
```

Before formatting anything, identify the external HDD carefully.

For example:

```text
sda   57.8G   SanDisk
sdb    1.8T   WD Elements
```

## 25. If the HDD already contains files

Do not format it.

Tell me what `FSTYPE` shows.

It may be:

```text
ntfs
ext4
exfat
```

We can mount whichever filesystem it already uses.

If it's empty and dedicated exclusively to the NAS, I'd use:

```text
ext4
```

## 26. Example: format an EMPTY HDD as ext4

Only do this if the HDD contains nothing you need.

Suppose the external disk is confirmed as:

```text
/dev/sdb
```

Partition it:

```sh
fdisk /dev/sdb
```

Inside fdisk:

```text
g
n
Enter
Enter
Enter
w
```

If this old machine has any trouble with GPT, we can use MBR instead, but GPT should generally be fine for a data disk.

Then format:

```sh
mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
```

## 27. Create your NAS mount point

```sh
mkdir -p /srv/storage
```

Get the HDD UUID:

```sh
blkid /dev/sdb1
```

You'll get something like:

```text
UUID="1234-abcd-..."
```

Edit:

```sh
vi /etc/fstab
```

Add:

```text
UUID=YOUR-UUID-HERE /srv/storage ext4 defaults,nofail 0 2
```

Mount:

```sh
mount -a
```

Verify:

```sh
df -h
```

## 28. Install Samba

Alpine's official Samba guide installs the package with:

```sh
apk add samba
```

citeturn626679search1

Create some folders:

```sh
mkdir -p /srv/storage/Shared
mkdir -p /srv/storage/Backups
mkdir -p /srv/storage/Media
```

For now:

```sh
chown -R utkarsh:utkarsh /srv/storage
```

## 29. Configure Samba

Back up the default config:

```sh
cp /etc/samba/smb.conf /etc/samba/smb.conf.bak
```

Then edit:

```sh
vi /etc/samba/smb.conf
```

Use this minimal configuration:

```ini
[global]
   workgroup = WORKGROUP
   server string = Alpine NAS
   security = user
   map to guest = Bad User

[storage]
   path = /srv/storage
   browseable = yes
   writable = yes
   valid users = utkarsh
   create mask = 0664
   directory mask = 0775
```

Create your Samba password:

```sh
smbpasswd -a utkarsh
```

Use a strong password.

Then enable Samba at boot:

```sh
rc-update add samba
```

Start it:

```sh
rc-service samba start
```

These service commands match Alpine's documented Samba setup. citeturn626679search1

## 30. Access from Windows

On your laptop press:

```text
Win + R
```

Enter:

```text
\\192.168.1.105\storage
```

Use the Alpine Samba credentials:

```text
Username: utkarsh
Password: <your Samba password>
```

If this works, your NAS is operational.

You can map it as a Windows drive:

```text
This PC
→ Map network drive
→ Z:
→ \\192.168.1.105\storage
```

Then it behaves almost like another local drive.

## 31. Reserve the server's IP

In your router, find:

```text
DHCP Reservation
Address Reservation
Static Lease
```

Reserve something like:

```text
192.168.1.50
```

for this PC's Ethernet MAC address.

Then you'll always use:

```text
\\192.168.1.50\storage
```

and:

```powershell
ssh utkarsh@192.168.1.50
```

## 32. What I would NOT install on this machine

With:

```text
504 MiB RAM
1-core Celeron
32-bit
```

keep it minimal.

Avoid:

```text
Nextcloud
Docker
Plex transcoding
Jellyfin
desktop GUI
RustDesk
heavy web dashboards
databases
AI software
```

Good workloads:

```text
Samba file storage
SSH
basic backup scripts
rsync
FTP/SFTP if needed
lightweight monitoring
```

Your final architecture should be:

```text
Windows laptop
   │
   ├── SSH
   │
   └── SMB
        │
        ▼
Old PC
├── Alpine Linux x86
├── 58GB SanDisk = OS
├── ~1GB swap
└── External HDD
     └── /srv/storage
```

I recommend doing this in two phases: first get **Alpine installed on the SanDisk and SSH working**, then stop and send me the output of `lsblk`, `free -h`, and `ip addr`. After that we can safely do the external HDD and Samba without risking your data.
